title: Samech
hookLine: the round letter of support, samach, to lean on

cards: Moses is near the end, and he asks God for a successor, someone to go out before the people so they won't be like sheep with no shepherd. God names Joshua and tells Moses: take him, and lay your hand on him.
Hand, singular. In Hebrew, yadecha, your hand. A few verses later we're told what Moses actually did.
In the King James words: "And he laid his hands upon him." Hands. Both of them.
He was asked for one and gave two.

teach.b: Samech. On the page it's nearly a closed circle. It makes a plain s, and its root, samach, means to lean on, to rest your weight against something.
Four ways in. First, the hands.
When Moses lays his hands on Joshua, the verb, vayismoch, is from that root. He isn't patting him on the head.
He's leaning on him, putting his own weight on the younger man's shoulders, as if to say: what held me up now rests on you.
The medieval commentator Rashi notices the change from one hand to two and says Moses did it generously, more than he was asked. Second, a name.

teach.h: SEMICHAH: HANDS THAT PASS IT ON.
teach.b: Rabbinic ordination is still called semichah, the same word: a teacher's authority, leaned onto a student. Third, the Temple.

In Leviticus, a person bringing an offering lays a hand on the animal's head before it is offered. Same verb. Some readers hear it this way: before you give something up, you lean on it and make it yours.

teach.h: A ROUND LETTER WITH NO GAP.
teach.b: Some teachers read samech's closed circle as support with no gap in it, a ring that holds whatever is inside. Yesterday samech was the verse that catches the one who fell.
Today it's the hand on a shoulder before anyone falls at all. Support, in Hebrew, isn't only rescue.

teach.h: AND HE LAID HIS HANDS UPON HIM.
teach.b: It's leaning in early, with both hands, and letting someone feel the weight of your trust.

how: Rabbinic ordination is called semichah, after Moses laying his hands on Joshua; Jewish students learn samech as the letter of the root meaning to lean on or support.

o: a letter whose name means a closed door
a round letter whose root means to lean on
the letter that begins the word for joy

p: ordination, the laying on of hands

s: God told Moses to lay both hands on Joshua
the instruction says your hand, singular. Moses laid both.
the word for rabbinic ordination comes from the same root as samech's verb
semichah, from samach, to lean on.
in Leviticus, a person bringing an offering leans a hand on it
the same verb: lay a hand on the animal's head before it's offered.

games.q: you're Moses. God names Joshua as the next leader and tells you to lay your hand on him. what do you do?
o: lay one hand, exactly as told.
send Joshua to the priest instead.
games.why: "and he laid his hands upon him": both hands. Rashi reads it as Moses giving more than he was asked.

practice: Feel what's holding you up right now, the chair, the floor, the wall at your back, and lean into it a little.

Then bring to mind someone carrying something new, a first job, a new baby, a new role, a hard diagnosis, and ask what both hands would look like for them: an hour of your time, a question you actually wait to hear answered.
If you pray, you can hold them in it.

wordCard.voice: Samech. The round letter whose root means to lean on, the root of semichah, the laying on of hands. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: leaning, laying on of hands — the word for rabbinic ordination.

carryVoice: Your line: samech supports. Both hands, not one. Go gently, and come back tomorrow.
